summary: Obstructive diseases make it hard to get air out: asthma, bronchiectasis, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema. Boards ask you to match each one to its mechanism and histology, read spirometry and DLCO, and use the blood gas to judge how sick an asthmatic really is.

points: Atopic asthma is a type I hypersensitivity driven by Th2 cells.
IL-4 switches B cells to IgE, IL-5 recruits and activates eosinophils, IL-13 drives mucus production.
Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells, releasing histamine and leukotrienes within minutes (early phase); eosinophils and Th2 cells sustain a late phase hours later.
Nonatopic triggers: viral infection, cold air, exercise, irritants, and aspirin.
Aspirin-exacerbated disease: blocking COX shunts arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes; often comes with nasal polyps.
Airway remodeling: goblet cell hyperplasia, thickened subepithelial basement membrane, submucosal gland enlargement, and smooth muscle hypertrophy.
Sputum: Curschmann spirals (coiled mucus casts with shed epithelium) and Charcot-Leyden crystals (from eosinophil protein).
Wheezing, prolonged expiration, tachypnea, use of accessory muscles.
Pulsus paradoxus: systolic pressure falls more than 10 mmHg on inspiration in a severe attack.
Obstruction is reversible: FEV1 rises after a bronchodilator.
Early gas: low PaCO2 and respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation, with hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch.
A normal or rising PaCO2 during an attack means the patient is tiring and nearing respiratory failure.
Permanent dilation of bronchi from obstruction plus necrotizing infection that destroys muscle and elastic tissue.
Causes: cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, tumor or foreign body, severe past pneumonia.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener when with situs inversus): dynein arm defect, sinusitis, infertility.
Daily cough with large amounts of foul purulent sputum, hemoptysis, clubbing.
Chronic infection can cause secondary (AA) amyloidosis.
Clinical definition: productive cough for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
Smoking causes mucous gland hyperplasia in the large bronchi and goblet cell metaplasia in small airways.
Reid index (gland layer thickness divided by wall thickness from epithelium to cartilage) above 0.5; normal is below about 0.4.
Blue bloater: early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, cyanosis, hypoxic vasoconstriction, then pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
Destruction of alveolar walls distal to the terminal bronchiole without significant fibrosis.
Protease and antiprotease imbalance: smoke recruits neutrophils and macrophages that release elastase, and oxidants inactivate alpha-1 antitrypsin.
Centriacinar: respiratory bronchioles destroyed, distal alveoli spared, upper lobes, smokers.
Panacinar: whole acinus, lower lobes, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (may also cause liver cirrhosis).
Paraseptal: distal acinus next to pleura and septa; subpleural bullae can rupture, causing spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
Lost elastic recoil lets small airways collapse on expiration, causing air trapping and a barrel chest.
Pink puffer: thin, dyspneic, breathes through pursed lips to keep airways open.
Obstruction: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 after a bronchodilator.
Air trapping raises TLC, residual volume, and FRC.
Emphysema: low DLCO because alveolar surface and capillaries are lost; gases near normal until late.
Chronic bronchitis: normal DLCO; early hypoxemia and hypercapnia from V/Q mismatch.

rows: Wheeze, Curschmann spirals, Charcot-Leyden crystals, eosinophils
Obstruction plus necrotizing infection, permanent dilation
Recurrent infection, AA amyloidosis, cor pulmonale
Mucous gland hyperplasia, Reid index above 0.5

charts.title: Emphysema patterns
rows: Cause often unknown; bullae in young adults

charts.title: Lung function in obstructive disease
rows: Low PaCO2 early; rising PaCO2 is danger

tricks.label: PaCO2 in the asthmatic
tricks.text: A breathless asthmatic should be blowing off CO2. If the PaCO2 is normal or climbing, the breathing muscles are failing, which is an emergency.

tricks.label: Bronchitis is blue, emphysema is pink
tricks.text: Chronic bronchitis wrecks V/Q matching early, so the patient is cyanotic and retains CO2. Emphysema loses alveoli and capillaries together, so matching is kept and the patient works hard to stay pink.

tricks.label: Alpha-1 hits lungs low and liver too
tricks.text: Panacinar, lower lobe emphysema in a young person, especially a nonsmoker, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. Check the liver for cirrhosis from the misfolded protein.

highYield: Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals in sputum mean asthma.
Reid index above 0.5 defines chronic bronchitis histologically.
Centriacinar emphysema is upper lobe and smoking; panacinar is lower lobe and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
Paraseptal emphysema bullae cause spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults.
COPD: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with increased TLC and residual volume.
DLCO is low in emphysema and normal in chronic bronchitis and asthma.
Bronchiectasis plus situs inversus and infertility suggests Kartagener syndrome.
Aspirin-exacerbated asthma comes with nasal polyps and leukotriene excess.
pitfalls: Asthma and COPD both lower FEV1/FVC; reversibility with a bronchodilator favors asthma.
A normal PaCO2 in an acute asthma attack is a warning sign and should not be read as reassurance.
Bronchiectasis is permanent airway dilation; chronic bronchitis has normal sized airways with excess mucus glands.
Air trapping raises TLC in obstructive disease; restrictive disease lowers TLC.

dumps.p: Trace an atopic asthma attack from inhaled allergen to narrowed airway. Then list the airway changes seen after years of disease.
l: Th2 cells release IL-4 (IgE switch), IL-5 (eosinophils), and IL-13 (mucus)
Allergen cross-links IgE on mast cells
Early phase: histamine and leukotrienes cause bronchoconstriction within minutes
Late phase: eosinophils and Th2 cells cause inflammation hours later
Remodeling: goblet cell hyperplasia, thick basement membrane, smooth muscle hypertrophy
Sputum: Curschmann spirals and Charcot-Leyden crystals
Nonatopic triggers: viral infection, cold air, exercise, aspirin

Chronic bronchitis histology: mucous gland hyperplasia, Reid index above 0.5
Emphysema: alveolar wall destruction from protease and antiprotease imbalance
Centriacinar upper lobes in smokers; panacinar lower lobes in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
Blue bloater: early hypoxemia and hypercapnia; pink puffer: gases near normal until late
DLCO low in emphysema, normal in chronic bronchitis
Both: FEV1/FVC below 0.7, increased TLC and residual volume
Chronic bronchitis leads to cor pulmonale

summary: Upper respiratory infections and inflammation run from the nose to the large bronchi. Boards ask you to tell the croup child from the epiglottitis child, strep throat from mono, and allergic from infectious rhinitis, and to predict the dangerous complications of sinusitis and strep pharyngitis.

points: Acute bronchitis: mostly viral, self-limited inflammation of the trachea and large bronchi.
Cough lasts up to about 3 weeks; chest radiograph shows no consolidation, which separates it from pneumonia.
Chronic bronchitis needs a productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years.
Acute laryngitis: usually viral or from voice overuse; hoarseness without stridor or a toxic child.
Croup: parainfluenza virus laryngotracheobronchitis, 6 months to 3 years old, barking cough, inspiratory stridor.
Croup film: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing) on a frontal neck radiograph.
Epiglottitis: classically Haemophilus influenzae type b in unvaccinated children; sudden high fever, drooling, dysphagia, muffled voice, tripod posture.
Epiglottitis film: thumb sign (swollen epiglottis) on lateral neck radiograph; the airway can close suddenly, so do not agitate the child or probe the throat.
Bacterial tracheitis: toxic child with high fever and thick purulent tracheal secretions, often Staphylococcus aureus, often after a viral illness.
Allergic rhinitis: type I hypersensitivity; IgE on mast cells, eosinophils in nasal secretions.
Pale, boggy, bluish turbinates, sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea; seasonal (pollens) or perennial (dust mites, animal dander).
Common cold: rhinovirus, a nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornavirus.
Rhinovirus is acid labile, so it does not survive the stomach, and grows best near 33 °C (91.4 °F) in the cool nose; the major group binds ICAM-1.
Vasomotor rhinitis: nonallergic, triggered by temperature change, odors, or spicy food; no IgE or eosinophils.
Mucosal swelling blocks the sinus ostium, trapping secretions; most cases follow a viral cold.
Bacterial causes: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (nontypeable), Moraxella catarrhalis.
Orbital cellulitis: ethmoid infection spreads through the thin lamina papyracea; proptosis, painful eye movement.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI), V1 and V2 numbness, headache, fever.
Mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis: Rhizopus or Mucor invade vessels, black necrotic tissue on palate or turbinates.
Streptococcus pyogenes: beta-hemolytic, bacitracin sensitive, group A; M protein resists phagocytosis.
Strep throat: fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical nodes, no cough.
Viral pharyngitis: cough, runny nose, hoarseness, conjunctivitis.
Rheumatic fever about 2 to 4 weeks after strep pharyngitis only: antibodies to M protein cross-react with heart proteins (molecular mimicry).
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis follows throat or skin infection: immune complex deposition, hematuria, edema, hypertension.
Mono (EBV infects B cells via CD21): exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly, fatigue.
Mono blood: atypical lymphocytes (reactive CD8 T cells) and heterophile antibodies (Monospot).
Peritonsillar abscess: severe one-sided throat pain, trismus, muffled hot potato voice, uvula pushed to the opposite side.

charts.title: Upper airway conditions
rows: Cough up to about 3 weeks, clear chest film
Drooling, muffled voice, tripod posture, thumb sign
Barking cough, inspiratory stridor, steeple sign
Viruses; S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis

tricks.label: Epiglottitis: the 4 Ds
tricks.text: Drooling, dysphagia, distress, and dysphonia (muffled voice) in a febrile child.

tricks.label: Steeple below, thumb above
tricks.text: Croup narrows the airway below the cords, so the frontal film looks like a steeple. Epiglottitis swells the structure above the cords, so the lateral film shows a thumb.

tricks.label: Rheumatic fever needs the throat
tricks.text: Rheumatic fever follows strep pharyngitis only. Glomerulonephritis can follow either throat or skin infection.

highYield: Thumb sign on lateral neck film means epiglottitis; steeple sign means croup.
Parainfluenza virus is the main cause of croup.
Rhinovirus is acid labile and binds ICAM-1; it is the main cause of the common cold.
Mucormycosis of the sinuses is a classic complication of diabetic ketoacidosis.
Strep throat: fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, and no cough.
Rheumatic fever arises from molecular mimicry between M protein and heart proteins.
Atypical lymphocytes in mono are reactive CD8 T cells; EBV itself infects B cells through CD21.
Peritonsillar abscess pushes the uvula away from the abscess and causes trismus.
pitfalls: Acute bronchitis has no consolidation; crackles and a new infiltrate mean pneumonia.
Both strep and mono cause exudative tonsillitis; posterior nodes, splenomegaly, and atypical lymphocytes point to mono.
Bacterial tracheitis can look like severe croup, but the child is toxic and has thick pus in the trachea.
Pale boggy mucosa with eosinophils is allergic; a red swollen mucosa with neutrophils fits infection.

summary: The pleural space can fill with air, blood, lymph, or fluid, and the lung can collapse from blockage or compression. Boards ask you to name the fluid from its lab values, predict which way the trachea moves, and recognize asbestos and chest trauma patterns.

points: Light criteria: exudate if pleural to serum protein above 0.5, pleural to serum LDH above 0.6, or pleural LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit.
Transudate (low protein, from pressure changes): heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome.
Exudate (leaky inflamed pleura): pneumonia, malignancy, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism, pancreatitis, autoimmune disease.
Chylothorax: thoracic duct disruption by trauma, surgery, or lymphoma; milky fluid, triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, chylomicrons.
Hemothorax: pleural fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit; from trauma, vessel rupture, or tumor.
Large hemothorax can cause hypovolemic shock; undrained clot organizes into fibrothorax that traps the lung.
Empyema: pus in the pleural space, usually after pneumonia.
Obstructive (resorption): a mucus plug, tumor, or foreign body blocks a bronchus and trapped air is absorbed into blood.
Resorption collapse pulls the mediastinum and trachea toward the collapsed side.
Compression atelectasis: fluid, air, or tumor pushes on the lung; mediastinum shifts away.
Contraction atelectasis: fibrosis prevents full expansion and is not reversible.
Exam: hyperresonance, absent or reduced breath sounds, reduced fremitus on the affected side.
Primary spontaneous: tall thin young men (often smokers) with ruptured apical subpleural blebs.
Secondary: underlying lung disease such as COPD or cystic fibrosis.
Tension: a one-way valve lets air in but not out; trachea shifts away, venous return falls, neck veins distend, blood pressure drops.
Pleural plaques: well-circumscribed, often calcified plaques on the parietal pleura and diaphragm; the most common asbestos lesion.
Also benign pleural effusion and diffuse pleural fibrosis; asbestosis itself is lower lobe interstitial fibrosis.
Ferruginous bodies: golden brown beaded fibers coated with iron-containing protein (Prussian blue positive).
Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most common cancer after asbestos exposure, and risk multiplies with smoking.
Mesothelioma risk rises with asbestos but is not linked to smoking.
Mediastinitis: esophageal perforation, infection after sternotomy, or inhalational anthrax (hemorrhagic, widened mediastinum).
Pneumomediastinum: air dissects into the mediastinum; subcutaneous crepitus and a Hamman crunch heard with each heartbeat.
Costochondritis: chest wall pain with reproducible tenderness over the costochondral junctions.
Flail chest: several adjacent ribs broken in two places; the segment moves inward on inspiration (paradoxical motion).
Pulmonary contusion: hemorrhage into alveoli with hypoxemia that worsens over the following hours.
Open pneumothorax: a penetrating wound lets air enter the pleural space with each breath.
Diaphragmatic rupture: more often on the left, so stomach or bowel appears in the left hemithorax.

charts.title: Pleural fluid types
rows: Many neutrophils, organisms, low glucose and pH
Fluid hematocrit at least half of blood hematocrit

charts.title: Which way does the trachea move?

tricks.label: Collapse pulls, mass pushes
tricks.text: When air leaves the lung (resorption atelectasis), the chest loses volume and the trachea is pulled toward that side. When something fills the chest (fluid, tension air), the trachea is pushed away.

tricks.label: Half the hematocrit means blood
tricks.text: Bloody looking fluid needs only a little blood. Call it a hemothorax only when the fluid hematocrit is at least half the blood hematocrit.

tricks.label: Asbestos plus smoking multiplies
tricks.text: Lung carcinoma risk from asbestos and smoking together is far higher than either alone. Mesothelioma risk does not change with smoking.

highYield: Exudate if any Light criterion is met: protein ratio above 0.5, LDH ratio above 0.6, or LDH above two thirds of the serum upper limit.
Chylothorax: milky fluid with triglycerides above 110 mg/dL from thoracic duct injury or lymphoma.
Tension pneumothorax: trachea away, hypotension, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds.
Resorption atelectasis shifts the mediastinum toward the collapse.
Calcified parietal pleural plaques are the most common sign of asbestos exposure.
Ferruginous bodies are iron-coated asbestos fibers.
Hamman crunch with subcutaneous crepitus means pneumomediastinum.
Flail chest moves paradoxically inward on inspiration.
pitfalls: Effusion and atelectasis are both dull to percussion; effusion pushes the trachea away and atelectasis pulls it toward.
Pulmonary embolism effusions are usually exudates, so do not assume all non-infectious effusions are transudates.
Pleural plaques are benign; they mark exposure and do not turn into mesothelioma.
Hyperresonance with absent breath sounds is pneumothorax; dullness with absent breath sounds is fluid or collapse.

dumps.p: Write Light criteria from memory. Then sort these into transudate or exudate and give one lab clue each: heart failure, pneumonia, cirrhosis, lung cancer, nephrotic syndrome, chylothorax, hemothorax.
l: Protein ratio above 0.5 means exudate
LDH ratio above 0.6 means exudate
Pleural LDH above two thirds of serum upper limit means exudate
Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome are transudates
Pneumonia and cancer cause exudates
Chylothorax: triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, chylomicrons
Hemothorax: fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit

dumps.p: Draw three chest outlines: obstructive atelectasis of the left lower lobe, a large left effusion, and a left tension pneumothorax. Show trachea position and label percussion and breath sounds.
l: Atelectasis: trachea pulled toward the left
Effusion: trachea pushed to the right, dull percussion
Tension pneumothorax: trachea pushed to the right, hyperresonant
Absent breath sounds on the affected side in tension pneumothorax
Tension pneumothorax lowers venous return: hypotension and distended neck veins
Resorption atelectasis cause: plug, tumor, or foreign body

summary: Pulmonary vascular disease covers fluid leaking into alveoli, clots and other material lodging in the pulmonary arteries, and high pressure in the pulmonary circuit. Boards ask you to use Starling forces, predict the blood gas in pulmonary embolism, tell fat, air, and amniotic emboli apart, and classify pulmonary hypertension.

points: Fluid leaves capillaries when hydrostatic pressure pushing out beats oncotic pressure pulling in, or when the capillary wall leaks.
Cardiogenic: left heart failure raises pulmonary capillary pressure; wedge pressure above 18 mmHg.
Chronic congestion leaves hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) in alveoli.
Noncardiogenic causes: capillary injury (ARDS), low plasma oncotic pressure (nephrotic syndrome, liver failure), lymphatic obstruction (tumor in lymphatics).
Noncardiogenic edema from capillary injury has a normal wedge pressure and protein-rich fluid.
Most emboli come from deep vein thrombosis of the leg veins above the knee.
Virchow triad: stasis (immobility, surgery, long travel), endothelial injury, hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, factor V Leiden).
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, tachypnea.
Blood gas: hypoxemia with low PaCO2 and respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.
Widened A-a gradient from V/Q mismatch and dead space.
D-dimer is sensitive but not specific; a normal value helps rule out embolism when suspicion is low.
A saddle embolus at the pulmonary artery bifurcation causes acute right heart strain (acute cor pulmonale) and can cause sudden death.
Most emboli do not infarct the lung because the bronchial arteries keep the tissue alive.
Infarction happens when a medium or small artery is blocked and bronchial flow is poor, as in left heart failure.
Wedge shaped and hemorrhagic (red), with the base on the pleura and the apex toward the hilum.
Causes hemoptysis and pleuritic pain from fibrinous pleuritis over the infarct.
Fat embolism: 24 to 72 hours after a long bone or pelvic fracture; hypoxemia, confusion, petechiae on chest, axillae, and conjunctivae.
Air embolism: air entering through a central venous catheter, or nitrogen bubbles forming in tissues and blood when a diver rises too fast (decompression sickness).
Amniotic fluid embolism: during labor or just after delivery; sudden dyspnea, hypotension, seizures, and DIC; fetal squamous cells found in maternal pulmonary vessels.
Defined by raised mean pulmonary artery pressure at rest (above about 20 mmHg by current criteria, 25 mmHg in older sources).
Group 1, pulmonary arterial hypertension: idiopathic or heritable (BMPR2 loss of function lets smooth muscle proliferate), drugs, connective tissue disease, HIV, shunts.
Group 2: left heart disease (most common cause overall).
Group 3: lung disease or hypoxia (COPD, interstitial disease, sleep apnea, altitude) through hypoxic vasoconstriction.
Group 4: chronic thromboembolic disease.
Vessels show medial hypertrophy, intimal fibrosis, and plexiform lesions in severe arterial disease; atherosclerosis appears in large pulmonary arteries.
Right ventricle hypertrophies, then fails (cor pulmonale): raised neck veins, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema.
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu): autosomal dominant; telangiectasias of skin and mucosa, nosebleeds, GI bleeding.
Pulmonary AVMs shunt blood right to left past the alveoli, causing hypoxemia that oxygen corrects poorly.
Clots and bacteria bypass the lung filter: paradoxical embolic stroke and brain abscess; AVMs can also cause hemoptysis.

Saddle embolus with acute right heart failure
Long bone or pelvic fracture, 24 to 72 hours later
Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, joint pain in divers

COPD, interstitial lung disease, sleep apnea

tricks.label: Two blood supplies protect the lung
tricks.text: The lung has pulmonary and bronchial arteries. An embolus usually causes hemorrhage without infarction unless the bronchial supply is also weak, as in heart failure.

tricks.label: Shunts ignore oxygen
tricks.text: Blood flowing through an AVM never meets alveolar air, so extra oxygen barely raises the PaO2. That clue separates a shunt from V/Q mismatch.

tricks.label: Fat embolism triad
tricks.text: Lungs, brain, skin: hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae a day or more after a femur fracture.

highYield: Cardiogenic edema: wedge pressure above 18 mmHg and heart failure cells.
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis, widened A-a gradient.
Saddle embolus causes acute cor pulmonale and sudden death.
Pulmonary infarcts are wedge-shaped, hemorrhagic, and pleural-based, usually with poor bronchial flow.
Fat embolism appears 24 to 72 hours after long bone fracture with a petechial rash.
Amniotic fluid embolism causes collapse and DIC during delivery.
BMPR2 mutation causes heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension; plexiform lesions are typical.
HHT pulmonary AVMs cause paradoxical stroke and brain abscess.
pitfalls: Most pulmonary emboli do not cause infarction, so a normal chest film does not rule out embolism.
Hypoxemia from a shunt improves little with oxygen; hypoxemia from V/Q mismatch improves well.
ARDS edema has a normal wedge pressure; a high wedge pressure points to the heart.
Cor pulmonale is right heart failure caused by lung or pulmonary vascular disease; right failure that follows left heart failure is a different label.

dumps.t: From leg clot to right heart failure

Source is usually deep veins of the leg above the knee
Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia
Hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis
Widened A-a gradient from V/Q mismatch
D-dimer raised but not specific
Saddle embolus causes acute right heart strain
Infarction only when bronchial flow is poor

dumps.p: Draw a pulmonary capillary next to an alveolus. Label the forces that move fluid out and in, then show what changes in heart failure, ARDS, nephrotic syndrome, and lymphatic blockage.

summary: This unit covers tumors from the nose to the pleura, plus esophageal cancer. Boards ask you to match each lung cancer to its location, histology, smoking link, and paraneoplastic syndrome, predict the local effects of tumor spread, and recognize the virus-linked head and neck cancers.

points: Adenocarcinoma: most common lung cancer overall and the most common in nonsmokers and women; peripheral, gland forming, mucin producing.
Adenocarcinoma in situ: lepidic growth along intact alveolar walls with no invasion (formerly bronchioloalveolar carcinoma).
Squamous cell: central, strongly tied to smoking; keratin pearls, intercellular bridges; may cavitate.
Large cell: peripheral, poorly differentiated with no glandular or squamous features; poor prognosis.
Small cell: central, almost always in smokers; small cells, scant cytoplasm, nuclear molding; chromogranin and synaptophysin positive.
Small cell spreads early, so it is usually beyond surgery at diagnosis.
Bronchial carcinoid: low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, nests of uniform cells, chromogranin positive, often a central polypoid mass in a younger patient, not tied to smoking.
Carcinoid can block a bronchus (atelectasis, recurrent pneumonia) and rarely causes carcinoid syndrome.
Squamous cell: PTHrP causes hypercalcemia.
Small cell: ACTH (Cushing syndrome) and ADH (SIADH with hyponatremia).
Small cell: Lambert-Eaton syndrome, antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels; weakness improves with repeated effort.
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (clubbing and periosteal new bone): especially adenocarcinoma.
Pancoast (superior sulcus) tumor: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from sympathetic chain invasion, and C8 to T1 brachial plexus deficits.
Superior vena cava syndrome: facial swelling and plethora, distended neck and chest veins, arm edema; usually a central tumor.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion: hoarseness (the left nerve loops under the aortic arch).
Phrenic nerve invasion: paralyzed, elevated hemidiaphragm.
Metastases are more common than primary lung cancer; they appear as multiple well-circumscribed nodules.
Hamartoma: most common benign lung tumor; cartilage and fat, popcorn calcification on imaging.
Mesothelioma: asbestos exposure decades earlier, no link to smoking; recurrent hemorrhagic effusion, tumor encasing the lung.
Mesothelioma markers: calretinin and cytokeratin positive; long slender microvilli on electron microscopy.
Metastatic adenocarcinoma in the pleura: calretinin negative, often CEA positive, short stubby microvilli.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma: EBV linked, more common in southern China and parts of Africa; nonkeratinizing or undifferentiated.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with neck node metastasis or one-sided serous otitis media from eustachian tube blockage.
Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma: smoking and alcohol; glottic tumors cause early hoarseness.
Vocal fold nodules: benign, bilateral, from voice overuse.
Juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis: HPV types 6 and 11, recurrent papillomas, hoarseness in children.
Nasal polyps: chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, aspirin-exacerbated disease with asthma, or cystic fibrosis in a child; cause obstruction and anosmia.
Vocal fold polyps: usually one-sided, from voice strain or smoking; cause hoarseness.
HPV 16 causes oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil and base of tongue, often in nonsmokers.
Tobacco and alcohol cause squamous carcinoma of the oral cavity and pharynx.
Squamous cell: upper and middle third; smoking, alcohol, very hot drinks, achalasia, nitrosamines.
Adenocarcinoma: distal third; GERD leading to Barrett esophagus, obesity.
Both cause progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids) and weight loss; invasion forward can create a tracheoesophageal fistula with cough on swallowing.

tricks.label: Popcorn is reassuring
tricks.text: A single round nodule with popcorn calcification and fat points to a hamartoma. Several round nodules of different sizes point to metastases from another organ.

tricks.label: Central tumors start with S
tricks.text: Squamous and small cell are the central lung cancers. Adenocarcinoma and large cell sit in the periphery.

tricks.label: Small cell makes hormones like a gland
tricks.text: Small cell tumors are neuroendocrine, so they can secrete ACTH and ADH and trigger antibodies that cross-react with nerve terminals (Lambert-Eaton).

highYield: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall and in nonsmokers.
Squamous cell carcinoma: central, keratin pearls, PTHrP hypercalcemia.
Small cell carcinoma: central, chromogranin positive, ACTH, ADH, Lambert-Eaton.
Pancoast tumor causes Horner syndrome and C8 to T1 deficits.
Mesothelioma: asbestos without smoking synergy, calretinin positive, long microvilli.
Metastases outnumber primary lung cancers; hamartoma shows popcorn calcification.
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is EBV linked; HPV 16 causes tonsil and base of tongue cancer.
Esophageal squamous cell is upper and middle; adenocarcinoma is distal with Barrett esophagus.
pitfalls: Carcinoid and small cell are both neuroendocrine and chromogranin positive; carcinoid is low grade with uniform cells and no smoking link.
Mesothelioma and pleural adenocarcinoma both cause bloody effusions; calretinin and long microvilli mark mesothelioma.
Vocal fold nodules are bilateral and from overuse; polyps are usually one-sided and tied to voice strain or smoking.
Adenocarcinoma is common in nonsmokers, but most adenocarcinomas still occur in smokers.

Large cell: peripheral, undifferentiated, poor prognosis

Small cell: ACTH, ADH, Lambert-Eaton, early metastasis

summary: Congenital lung disease ranges from a single gene defect (cystic fibrosis) to errors in how the foregut, diaphragm, and lung buds form. Boards ask you to explain the CFTR chloride defect in sweat and airway, predict its many organ effects, and recognize tracheoesophageal fistula, diaphragmatic hernia, sequestration, and bronchogenic cyst in a newborn or child.

points: Autosomal recessive mutation in CFTR on chromosome 7; most common is deletion of phenylalanine 508 (F508del).
F508del misfolds the protein, which is degraded before it reaches the cell surface.
CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel; cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates CFTR so ATP can open it.
Sweat duct: CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride, and sodium follows; without it both stay in the sweat, so sweat is salty.
Airway: CFTR normally secretes chloride and restrains ENaC; without it chloride secretion falls and sodium absorption through ENaC rises.
Water follows the sodium out of the airway lumen, so airway surface liquid is depleted and mucus becomes thick and hard to clear.
Newborn: meconium ileus (thick meconium blocks the ileum).
Pancreatic insufficiency: steatorrhea, poor growth, deficiency of vitamins A, D, E, and K.
Lungs: early Staphylococcus aureus, later mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa; bronchiectasis and clubbing.
Sinuses: chronic sinusitis and nasal polyps; nasal polyps in a child should prompt CF testing.
Most men are infertile from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.
Diagnosis: sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or higher.
The foregut fails to separate fully into trachea and esophagus.
Most common form: esophageal atresia (blind upper pouch) with a distal fistula from trachea to the lower esophagus.
Fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid, causing polyhydramnios.
Newborn drools and chokes, coughs, and turns cyanotic with the first feeds.
A nasogastric tube will not pass and coils in the upper pouch; air in the stomach shows the distal fistula.
Look for VACTERL: vertebral, anal atresia, cardiac, tracheoesophageal fistula, esophageal atresia, renal, and limb (radial) defects.
Pleuroperitoneal fold (membrane) fails to close, usually on the left posterolateral side (Bochdalek).
Abdominal contents enter the chest and compress the developing lung, causing pulmonary hypoplasia.
Newborn: severe respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the chest, heart sounds shifted to the right.
Pulmonary sequestration: nonfunctioning lung tissue with no bronchial connection, supplied by a systemic artery from the aorta.
Sequestration is usually in a lower lobe and becomes infected again and again.
Bronchogenic cyst: abnormal budding of the foregut; fluid-filled cyst lined by respiratory epithelium, usually in the mediastinum near the carina.
Bronchogenic cysts can compress an airway or become infected.

tricks.label: Sweat goes the other way
tricks.text: In most tissues CFTR pushes chloride out, so CF makes secretions dry. In the sweat duct CFTR pulls chloride back in, so CF makes sweat salty. Same broken channel, opposite direction.

tricks.label: VACTERL
tricks.text: Vertebral defects, Anal atresia, Cardiac defects, Tracheo-Esophageal fistula with esophageal atresia, Renal anomalies, Limb (radial) defects.

tricks.label: Sequestration is fed by the aorta
tricks.text: If a lung mass has its own artery from the aorta and no airway connection, it is a sequestration. A bronchogenic cyst is a fluid sac from the foregut, usually in the mediastinum.

highYield: Cystic fibrosis: autosomal recessive CFTR mutation, F508del misfolding.
Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or higher confirms cystic fibrosis.
Increased ENaC sodium absorption dries the airway surface liquid in cystic fibrosis.
Men with cystic fibrosis are usually infertile from absent vas deferens.
Esophageal atresia with distal fistula: polyhydramnios, choking with feeds, gastric air bubble.
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: left posterolateral, scaphoid abdomen, pulmonary hypoplasia.
Pulmonary sequestration has a systemic arterial supply from the aorta.
pitfalls: Salty sweat comes from failed chloride reabsorption in the sweat duct, so sweat chloride rises even though the airway is dry.
A gasless abdomen suggests esophageal atresia without a distal fistula; air in the stomach means the distal fistula is present.
Sequestration has no bronchial connection; a bronchogenic cyst arises from the foregut and is usually mediastinal.
The danger in diaphragmatic hernia is the small, underdeveloped lung (pulmonary hypoplasia); moving the bowel back does not fix it.

dumps.p: Draw an airway cell and a sweat duct cell side by side. Show CFTR and ENaC with arrows for chloride, sodium, and water, first in health and then in cystic fibrosis.
l: CFTR is an ATP-gated chloride channel regulated by cAMP and protein kinase A
Airway: CFTR secretes chloride into the lumen
Airway in CF: less chloride secretion, more sodium absorbed through ENaC
Water leaves the airway lumen, so mucus thickens
Sweat duct: CFTR reabsorbs chloride and sodium follows
Sweat duct in CF: chloride and sodium stay in sweat
Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or higher

TE fistula: VACTERL association
Diaphragmatic hernia: failed pleuroperitoneal fold closure, left posterolateral
Diaphragmatic hernia: scaphoid abdomen, pulmonary hypoplasia
Sequestration: systemic artery from aorta, no airway connection, recurrent infection
Bronchogenic cyst: foregut budding, fluid-filled, mediastinal

summary: This unit covers infections of the lungs and airways, from common pneumonias to tuberculosis, fungi, and childhood infections like pertussis and RSV. Boards ask you to match the organism to the patient and the pattern on imaging, follow tuberculosis from primary to reactivation, and predict toxin effects and complications.

points: Lobar: consolidation of a whole lobe; Streptococcus pneumoniae most often, also Klebsiella (alcoholism, currant jelly sputum).
Lobar stages: congestion, red hepatization (red cells, neutrophils, fibrin), gray hepatization (red cells broken down), resolution.
Consolidation exam: dullness, increased tactile fremitus, egophony, bronchial breath sounds.
Bronchopneumonia: patchy, often multilobar, centered on bronchioles; Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas.
Atypical (interstitial): patchy interstitial infiltrates that look worse than the patient; dry cough, headache, myalgia.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae: no cell wall, cold agglutinins (IgM), young adults in close quarters such as dorms and barracks.
Others: Chlamydia pneumoniae, viruses, and Legionella (water aerosols, high fever, diarrhea, confusion, hyponatremia).
Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia: Pseudomonas, MRSA, and enteric gram-negative rods.
Chemical pneumonitis is sterile acid injury within hours of aspirating gastric contents; aspiration pneumonia is infection by oral bacteria over days in dependent segments.
Lung abscess: aspiration of oral anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, Peptostreptococcus) in alcoholism, seizures, or dysphagia.
Abscess shows an air-fluid level, often in the right lung (posterior upper lobe or superior lower lobe if supine), with foul sputum; Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella also cause abscess.
Primary: Ghon focus in the lower upper lobe or upper lower lobe plus a hilar node (Ghon complex).
Th1 cells release IFN-gamma that activates macrophages; caseating granulomas wall off the bacilli, leaving latent infection.
Tuberculin skin test: type IV reaction read at 48 to 72 hours; can be positive after BCG vaccine.
IFN-gamma release assay: T cell response to antigens not in BCG, so BCG does not cause a false positive.
Reactivation: apical cavitation, fever, night sweats, weight loss, hemoptysis; risk rises with HIV and immunosuppression.
Miliary spread: tiny seed-like nodules in kidneys, meninges, adrenals, and vertebrae (Pott disease).
Endemic dimorphic fungi grow as molds in soil and yeasts (or spherules) in tissue; they infect healthy hosts.
Histoplasma: Ohio and Mississippi valleys, bird and bat droppings, tiny yeasts inside macrophages.
Blastomyces: similar region, broad-based budding yeast; spreads to skin and bone.
Coccidioides: southwestern US deserts, spherules with endospores; spreads to skin, bone, and meninges.
All three form granulomas that can mimic tuberculosis.
Pneumocystis: CD4 below 200 per microliter, bilateral ground-glass infiltrates, hypoxemia on exertion, high LDH.
Aspergillus: aspergilloma in an old cavity, angioinvasive disease in neutropenia, allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis in asthma and cystic fibrosis.
Pertussis stages: catarrhal (cold-like, most contagious), paroxysmal (coughing fits, inspiratory whoop, posttussive vomiting), convalescent.
Pertussis toxin causes marked lymphocytosis; young infants may have apnea instead of a whoop, and pneumonia.
RSV: most common cause of infant bronchiolitis and pneumonia; winter epidemics with wheezing and tachypnea; severe in prematurity, congenital heart disease, and chronic lung disease.
Diphtheria: gray adherent pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped, bull neck nodes; grows on tellurite agar, Elek test shows toxin.
Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2; it causes myocarditis, heart block, and cranial and peripheral neuropathy.
Influenza destroys ciliated epithelium, opening the door to secondary Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.
Avian and human influenza strains can swap gene segments (reassortment) and create novel pandemic strains.
Coronaviruses: some cause common colds; SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 cause severe pneumonia.
SARS-CoV-2 enters cells through ACE2 on airway and alveolar cells; loss of smell, diffuse alveolar damage, and thrombosis; risk rises with age and comorbidity.
Inhalational anthrax: hemorrhagic mediastinitis with a widened mediastinum.
Tularemia: rabbits and ticks. Q fever: Coxiella from farm animal birth products. Melioidosis: Burkholderia pseudomallei in Southeast Asia.

tricks.label: Ghon is primary, apex is reactivation
tricks.text: Primary TB lands in the middle of the lung near the fissure with a hilar node. Reactivation favors the apex, where oxygen is high, and cavitates.

tricks.label: Legionella hints
tricks.text: Pneumonia plus diarrhea, confusion, and low sodium in an older patient exposed to water aerosols such as cooling towers points to Legionella.

tricks.label: Where aspiration goes
tricks.text: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical. Lying down, aspirate falls into the posterior right upper lobe and superior right lower lobe; standing, into the right lower lobe bases.

highYield: Lobar stages: congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, resolution.
Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall and causes cold agglutinins in young adults.
Ghon complex: subpleural Ghon focus plus hilar node.
IFN-gamma release assay is not affected by BCG vaccination.
Pneumocystis: CD4 below 200, ground-glass infiltrates, high LDH.
Diphtheria toxin inactivates EF-2 and causes myocarditis and neuropathy.
Influenza is followed by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.
Inhalational anthrax causes a widened, hemorrhagic mediastinum.
pitfalls: Atypical pneumonia often looks worse on the film than the patient looks at the bedside; in lobar pneumonia the patient is acutely ill with dense consolidation.
A positive skin test after BCG may be false; use the IFN-gamma release assay.
Chemical pneumonitis starts within hours and is sterile; bacterial aspiration pneumonia develops over days.
Aspergilloma lives in an old cavity in a normal host; angioinvasive aspergillosis is in neutropenic patients.
